paragraphs.source_en: Perhaps, after Tsangyang Gyatso became the Dalai Lama, within those deep palace courtyards he came to understand all the more the preciousness of feeling, and without turning back dissolved himself into that sea of passionate entanglement. Perhaps, after emerging from the whirlpool of struggles for power, he understood more deeply the sanctity of feeling, and without regret entered into that long tenderness of women’s love, letting the jade-like nectar of emotion submerge him.

paragraphs.source_en: The Sixth Dalai Lama held office from 1708 to 1710; it may truly be called a moment that vanished in an instant, while only the Love Songs of Tsangyang Gyatso, like the waters of Qinghai Lake, have flowed fragrant through the generations and carried their fame afar. For nearly three hundred years and more, these love songs have lingered on the lips of the Tibetan and Mongol peoples; they may truly be said to be known in every household, growing ever fresher with time. The Love Songs of Tsangyang Gyatso are the most popular love songs on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau; The Love Songs of Tsangyang Gyatso are the folk songs that have sunk most deeply into the hearts of the people of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. Tsangyang Gyatso’s talent and feeling have, for hundreds and thousands of years, still hung like mist over the vast waves of Qinghai Lake. Because of Qinghai Lake, Tsangyang Gyatso gained another kind of life, an eternal life.

paragraphs.source_zh: 六世达赖一七○八年至一七一○年在职，真可以说是转瞬即逝，唯有《仓央嘉措情歌》与青海湖水一般世代流芳，声名远播。近三百多年来，这些情歌一直在藏族蒙族人民的口头萦绕真可谓家喻户晓，历久弥新。《仓央嘉措情歌》是青藏高原最流行的情歌；《仓央嘉措情歌》是青藏高原最深入人心的民歌。仓央嘉措的才情，千百年来还氤氲在青海湖的烟波浩渺中。仓央嘉措因青海湖而得到另一种生命，一种永恒的生命。

paragraphs.source_en: Because the Yellow Hat school of Tibetan Buddhism founded by the Qinghai native Tsongkhapa exerted immense political influence across Central Asia, West Asia, and the Far East, the lofty position of the Khoshut tribe aroused the jealousy of another Kalmyk tribe, the Choros within Dzungaria, whose leader Tsering Dondub led troops into Tibet. Lhazang Khan defended the Potala Palace to the very end and was killed while fleeing. Thus the Khoshut protectorate over Tibet came to an end. And Lhazang Khan, too, vanished without a trace amid the struggle for power. When people sing Tsangyang Gyatso’s “la’i” again and again, no one any longer mentions that Lhazang Khan who once dominated his age. The one truly buried in the mists of history was not the Sixth Dalai Lama, but Lhazang Khan, who drove him to his death.

paragraphs.source_en: Tsangyang Gyatso’s life story added still more romantic and mysterious color to his love poems. The classic Lhasa Tibetan woodblock edition of Tsangyang Gyatso’s Love Poems gathers more than sixty of his love poems. Today they have been translated into more than twenty languages and have spread almost throughout the world, with new translations appearing one after another. Among the people, however, there are more than two hundred love poems attributed to Tsangyang Gyatso. In Tibet today, many people can sing songs adapted from his poems.

paragraphs.source_en: Tsangyang Gyatso’s full name was Losang Rinchen Tsangyang Gyatso, meaning “Ocean of Auspicious Wisdom, Jewel, and Brahma Sound,” or “Ocean of Brahma Sound”; on the sixteenth day of the first month in the twenty-second year of the Kangxi reign of the Qing dynasty, 1683, he was born in Yusong in the Monyul region of southern Tibet, to a father named Tashi Tenzin and a mother named Tsewang Lhamo. It is said that around the fifteenth year of Kangxi, while traveling through Qinghai on his way to the capital to request imperial approval, he died of illness at the age of twenty-four; another account says this cannot be verified and that the year of his death is unknown.
